- From the Shewan highlands to the Lake Tana area under King Minas.
- This was due to the expansion of the Oromo south of the Abay River.
Factors for Instability:
- Continued Oromo expansion.
- Ottoman Turks occupied Massawa (1557) and advanced into the interior.
- Rivalry between the monarch and warlords.
Attempts at Consolidation:
- The Lake Tana region was agriculturally fertile and important for trade.
- Permanent structures were built (e.g., Guzara under Sertse Dingil).

slides.title: The Imposition of Catholicism
content: Background: Portugal and the Pope wanted to convert Ethiopia to Catholicism.
Jesuit Missionaries:
- Arrived in Ethiopia with the goal of converting the people.
- Pedro Paez was successful in converting King Susenyos.
King Susenyos (r. 1607-32):
- Made Catholicism the official state religion (1622).
- Harsh measures led to peasant rebellions.
Fasiledes (r. 1632-1667):
- Restored Orthodox Christianity.
- Expelled the Jesuits.
- Introduced a closed-door policy to prevent foreign interference.

slides.title: The Gondarine Period (1636-1769)
content: Fasiledes established Gondar as a permanent capital in 1636.
Magnificent castles and churches were built.
Gondar became the center of political, intellectual, religious, and economic life.
Culture: Church paintings, music, poetry, calligraphy flourished.
Trade: Gondar controlled trade routes and had a famous market.
Communities: Muslims, Bete-Israel, and expatriates lived in separate quarters.
Important Rulers: Fasiledes, Yohannis I, Iyasu I ('the Great'), and later Bekaffa.
Iyasu I: Revised the Fitha Negest, reorganized taxes and customs.
Empress Mintiwab:
- A prominent woman in the politics of the kingdom.
- Secured power for her son and organized the Quaregnoch faction.

slides.title: The Zemene Mesafint (Era of the Warlords, 1769-1855)
content: Definition: A period of weakening central authority and the rise of powerful regional lords.
Causes:
- The wars of Imam Ahmad eroded the power of the monarchy.
- The establishment of a permanent capital (Gondar) led to the neglect of provinces.
Characteristics:
- Kings in Gondar were puppets of regional lords.
- Political disintegration: Tigray, Simien, Dembiya, Begemdir, Lasta, Amhara, Yejju, Wollo, Gojjam, and Shewa.
- Constant power struggles and civil wars.
- The Yejju Oromo held the title of Rasbitweded.
Effects:
- Decline in agricultural production, stagnation in trade, collapse of handicrafts.
- Hardship for the peasantry.
End: The period ended when Kasa Hailu (Tewodros II) defeated the regional lords and was crowned emperor in 1855.

slides.title: The Kingdom of Shewa and European Travelers
content: Kingdom of Shewa:
- Founded by Negasi Kirstos (end of the 17th century).
- Political centers: Ayne, Doqaqit, Ankober.
- Remained independent during the Zemene Mesafint.
- Reached its peak under Nigus Sahle Sellassie (r. 1813-1847).
European Travelers and Explorers (since 1805):
- Motives: Adventure, religious zeal (missionaries), scientific research, and trade.
- Key Travelers: Henry Salt, Samuel Gobat, C.W. Isenburg, Captain W.C. Harris, Walter Plowden.
Treaties:
- 1841: Treaty of commerce and friendship between Harris and Sahle Sellassie.
- 1849: Treaty of friendship between Plowden and Ras Ali II.

sections.section_title: The Industrial Revolution and its Political, Economic and Social Effects on Europe

slides.title: The Industrial Revolution: Causes and Effects
content: The Industrial Revolution (mid-18th century): A shift from manual labor to machine-made goods.
Agricultural Revolution: Preceded the Industrial Revolution.
- Wealthy landowners enclosed land, improved farming methods.
- Seed drill (c. 1701), crop rotation, and livestock breeding increased food production.
Why in England?
- Natural resources: Water, coal, iron ore.
- Expanding economy, banking system.
- Political stability and favorable laws.
Key Inventions:
- Textile: Flying shuttle, spinning jenny, water frame, spinning mule, power loom.
- Cotton gin (Eli Whitney, 1793).
- Steam engine (James Watt).
- Transportation: Steamboat (Robert Fulton), railroads (George Stephenson).

slides.title: Social and Economic Impacts
content: Positive Effects:
- Urbanization (city building).
- Created jobs, increased wealth.
- Technological progress and invention.
- Mass production of goods.
- Healthier diets, better housing, cheaper clothing.
Negative Effects:
- Unhealthy working conditions.
- Air and water pollution.
- Child labor.
- Class tensions: Middle class (factory owners) and working class (laborers).
Responses to Industrialization:
- Luddite Movement: Workers smashed machines.
- Laissez-faire: Free market economy (Adam Smith).
- Socialism: Government should intervene to improve people's lives (Charles Fourier, Saint-Simon).
- Marxism: Radical type of socialism (Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels).

slides.title: The American War of Independence: Causes and Course
content: Background: Britain had 13 colonies in North America.
Immediate Causes:
- 'Taxation without representation' (Stamp Act of 1765).
- Boston Tea Party (1773).
- Intolerable Acts, including closing Boston Harbor.
The Course of the War:
- First Continental Congress (1774).
- Fighting erupted at Lexington and Concord (April 19, 1775).
- Second Continental Congress, raised army under George Washington.
- Declaration of Independence (July 4, 1776).
Why did the colonists win?
- Stronger motivation.
- Overconfident British generals.
- The expense of fighting an overseas war.
- French assistance from 1778.
Effects:
- Liberated American colonies from British rule.
- Created the United States of America.
- Influenced the French and Latin American revolutions.

slides.title: Causes of the French Revolution
content: Causes of the French Revolution:
Long-term Causes:
- Absolutism (divine right of kings).
- Unjust socio-political system (Old Regime).
- Influence of Enlightenment philosophes.
- System of mercantilism.
Short-term Causes:
- Poor harvests left peasants with little money for taxes.
- Influence of successful revolutions (England, America).
- Bankruptcy (deficit spending).
- Great Fear, worst famine in memory.
French Society Divided into Three Estates:
- First Estate: High-ranking Church members (privileged).
- Second Estate: Nobility (privileged).
- Third Estate: Peasants, artisans, city workers, bourgeoisie (unprivileged).

slides.title: Phases of the French Revolution
content: Phases of the Revolution:
1. National Assembly (1789-1791):
- Tennis Court Oath.
- Storming of the Bastille (July 14, 1789).
- Abolished feudal privileges.
- Declaration of the Rights of Man.
- Constitution of 1791.
2. Legislative Assembly (1791-1792):
- War against Austria and Prussia.
3. The Convention (1792-1795):
- First French Republic established.
- Reign of Terror (1793-1794):
- Led by the Committee of Public Safety.
- 15,000 guillotined.
- Ends with Robespierre's fall.
4. The Directory (1795-1799):
- A new government.

slides.title: Key Reforms and Consequences
content: Key Reforms:
- Abolition of special privileges.
- Declaration of the Rights of Man: Liberty, equality, fraternity.
- Equality before the law.
- Reforms in local government.
- Taxes based on ability to pay.
Women in the Revolution:
- Olympe de Gouges: Declaration of the Rights of Woman.
- Women gained some rights (inheritance, easier divorce).
Consequences:
- Spread of revolutionary ideas.
- Rise of nationalism.
The revolution ended with Napoleon's rise to power in 1799.

slides.title: Napoleon Bonaparte: Reforms and Empire
content: Napoleon Bonaparte (1769-1821): A French military genius from Corsica.
Rise to Power: Took power in 1799 as First Consul, declared himself Emperor in 1804.
Major Reforms:
- Napoleon Code (1804): Codified French law, emphasized private property.
- Bank of France (1800).
- Concordat of 1801: Agreement with the Catholic Church.
- Educational reforms: State-controlled public education.
- Rewarded talent (meritocracy).
Repressive Measures:
- Severe inequality for women.
- Banned trade unions.
- Police state to suppress opposition.
Napoleon's Empire: Conquered most of Europe.
- Key Battles: Trafalgar (1805), Leipzig (1813).

slides.title: The Congress of Vienna and Napoleon's Legacy
content: Napoleon's Downfall:
- Defeated at the Battle of Leipzig (1813).
- Abdicated in 1814, exiled to Elba.
- Returned for the 'Hundred Days' in 1815.
- Finally defeated at the Battle of Waterloo, exiled to St. Helena.
Congress of Vienna (1814-1815):
- Key Representatives: Metternich (Austria), Castlereagh (Britain), Alexander I (Russia), Talleyrand (France).
Principles of Settlement:
- Legitimacy: Restoring old dynasties.
- Compensation: Rewarding states that helped defeat Napoleon.
- Balance of Power: Prevent any one state from dominating Europe.
Napoleon's Legacy:
- Positive: Consolidated revolutionary institutions, spread French reforms.
- Negative: Repressive rule, caused enormous suffering.
